sentences.text: Gettyia is known from a single fossilized right tarsometatarsus bone.
This known bone is similar to those of other North American avisaurids but is much smaller in size.
The bird possessed a knob-like structure on the front edge of its second metatarsal that connected to the tibialis cranialis muscle.
The third and fourth metatarsals were more extensively fused than in other avisaurids, with fusion occurring near both the ankle and the toes.
The specific name gloriae honors Gloria Siebrecht, a volunteer fossil collector who discovered the original specimen.
The position of the tibialis cranialis tubercule suggests that Gettyia had a more specialized lifestyle than other avisaurids.
The species was originally described as Avisaurus gloriae in 1995 based on a single tarsometatarsus fossil found in Glacier County, Montana.
The genus Gettyia was established by Atterholt and colleagues in 2018.
Birds of prey utilize forceful flexion during their hunting behavior.
Arboreal parrots and climbing birds use forceful flexion to maintain stability while foraging or hanging from branches.
More terrestrial birds typically require speed over force to assist with locomotion like walking and hopping.
Gettyia is an extinct genus of avialan belonging to the clade Enantiornithes and the family Avisauridae that lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous.
Gettyia is an extinct genus of enantiornithean bird belonging to the family Avisauridae.
Gettyia is a monotypic genus known only from the species G. gloriae.
Gettyia is classified within the family Avisauridae.
Fossils of Gettyia date to the late Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.
Gettyia inhabited both humid low-lying swamps near the Western Interior Seaway and the drier uplands leading to the Rocky Mountains.
